# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

insights.line: What would make it worth more

whys.g1: The groups are plain and most answers sit where I'd put them, but Trevor actually knows his cost (about six hundred a month in overtime) and is setting a price ceiling, so he's a slightly odd fit under 'no proven time or cost saved'.
whys.g2: There are no junk, explicit or off-topic answers on this line; all seven are about price and what the tool is worth.

whys.g1: All three grouped answers are about a per-site price that doesn't pay for itself, the name is plain, and the two left out (wanting a free trial first, and not trusting an app with the legal record) are different objections that don't belong in that group.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line; all five are real reasons about buying it.

whys.g1: These are two different reasons, one that a per-site fee adds up across jobs and pricing by active supers would earn more, the other that supers lose too little time on logs to justify paying, so leaving them ungrouped is right and no group or name is wrong.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so it scores 2 by default.

founder.order_why: It runs the way I'd explain Fresco, from where it applies and the superintendent's log problem to the idea, then who pays at the contractor, and only then who to send it to.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 20 and 22 overlap: my first real step is already a paid pilot on one site, and then I'm asked whether to offer a pilot. Screens 14 and 17 also overlap a little, because the CFO's sign-off and the security review are both people who must agree and things that could slow a purchase.
founder.missing: No screen title asks what the price is charged per; mine is per site per month with unlimited users, and multi-site or multi-month discounts, which matters when a contractor runs many jobs. None asks whether it must work with the Procore or ACC setup the contractor already has, which could decide the sale, though these may be covered inside the cards I can't see from the titles.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It goes from whether my jobs qualify, to the idea, to hours and price, then budget, sign-off and trial, and ends on the pilot decision, which is how I'd think it through.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Whether it pushes logs and photos into Procore or ACC without double entry, and whether the price holds across all users on a site, since per-seat limits would change what I'd pay.

screens.why1: Right after who has to agree and whether the buyer pays, it makes sense to ask what holds up a contractor's purchase before testing whether they'd buy.
screens.why2: The question is short and the hint's approvals, reviews, procurement and switching are all words I hear when selling to general contractors.
screens.why3: I know this from selling to GCs: they want a trial on a live job, a check that it works with Procore, and a security review.
screens.why4: The box takes my own list, and 'Leave this out of the study' is a fair way out if I don't want to test friction.
screens.why5: I typed three steps, but Keel's belief keeps only the trial, drops Procore and security without saying so, and makes my routine pilot step sound like the main thing that could kill the deal.
screens.instead: Keep the question, and have Keel write: 'A trial on one live job, a Procore check or a security review can slow or stop the purchase; we'll test the trial first, is that the right one?'

screens.why1: Right after I said what could slow or stop a purchase, it is obvious why Keel plays those steps back for me to check before they go into the study.
screens.why2: Live job, Procore, security review and budget approval are all everyday words in selling to a general contractor, and the belief reads clean on first pass.
screens.why3: I sell these pilots to contractors, so I know first-hand that a trial on one job, the Procore check and the security review are where deals stall.
screens.why4: These are the real hurdles and none is nonsense, but the Procore check overlaps with the trial because that is where we would prove the push works, and no row covers supers or the field team refusing to use it.
screens.why5: The trial, Procore check and security review are mine, but budget approval is an extra row I did not name as a step, and the belief puts all the weight on the trial, which is also how I get customers in the door.
screens.instead: Which of these is most likely to slow or stop you buying this? A trial on one live job / A check that it works with Procore / A security review / A budget approval / Getting the supers on the job to use it

screens.why1: Right after I listed and checked what could slow a purchase, it is obvious why Keel asks me to pick the one step to test.
screens.why2: Trial, Procore check, security review and budget approval are all plain to me, but the bar packs two conditions into one line ('needed and would take a long time'), and the screen has no direct question, so I need a second read to see what I am choosing.
screens.why3: Selling to general contractors, I know these are the steps a deal goes through, and I can say which one I believe holds things up.
screens.why4: The four are real steps in my words, but a trial on a live job and a Procore check overlap because the trial is usually where Procore fit gets proven, and there is no 'something else' option.
screens.why5: The trial and 'slow or stop' are what I meant, but the bar tests only 'needed and takes a long time', which misses a contractor who flatly refuses a trial and so stops the purchase quickly.
screens.instead: Which one step do you most believe slows or stops a contractor buying? A trial on one live job / A check that it works with Procore / A security review / A budget approval / Something else. Holds if at least 2 in 3 say this step would be needed and would hold up or stop the purchase.

screens.why1: After who decides, what it costs, the price and what slows a purchase, asking what first commitment I want from the buyer is the obvious last commercial question.
screens.why2: "First real step" with the hint about time, data, money or a signature is immediately clear to a founder selling to general contractors, and I can answer it in my own words.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I want from a contractor first, since we charge per site per month and a paid pilot on one live job is how I would start.
screens.why4: The free-text box lets me state my own step, and "Leave this out of the study" is a fitting escape if I do not want to test commitment.
screens.why5: My words "start a paid pilot on one site" are kept, but the belief adds "In most cases" and "now", which claim more certainty and urgency than I typed, and a pilot would follow the Procore check and security review I listed rather than happen now.

screens.why1: Right after I named the paid pilot as the first real step, it makes sense for Keel to show that step back as the last commercial belief to check.
screens.why2: The sentence is clear, but 'in most cases' next to 'now' takes a second read, and 'holds if no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no' needs a moment of working out.
screens.why3: I sell to general contractors and offer per-site terms, so I can judge whether an ops lead would start a paid pilot on one job.
screens.why4: The bar is workable and the only answers it names are 'probably not' and 'no', which is fair, but it does not say how a 'not until the CFO and a Procore check clear it' answer counts, and that is the likely true answer for a contractor.
screens.why5: It keeps my step 'start a paid pilot on one site', but 'now' drifts a little because it skips the trial, Procore check and security review I listed as purchase steps.
screens.instead: Belief: Most contractor operations leads would start a paid pilot on one site once it clears their usual checks. Holds if no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no.

screens.why1: I just named a paid pilot as my first real step, so being asked before launch whether to offer it to the people who say yes is an obvious next question.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is a word I use every day with contractors, and the question and hint are clear on first reading, even though I haven't seen the Pilot tab yet.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads from this study is entirely my own call, and I can make it immediately.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the whole choice, the two options are distinct, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: I typed "Start a paid pilot on one site", but the line shown says only "try this for real", which drops both paid and one site, so a yes could be weaker than the commitment I want.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you start a paid pilot on one site? Leave your email." Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, choosing who asks my questions on the AI link is an obvious last setup step.
screens.why2: I get the choice at once, but "Tap the other face to hear her and pick her instead" reads oddly next to two bare names, and "uses 400 credits" leaves me a second read to work out whether picking or recording costs that.
screens.why3: I can listen to two voices and pick the one my supers would stay on with, with no outside knowledge needed.
screens.why4: Two distinct faces and a default are enough, but the bare names tell me nothing until I tap, and there is no way to see a choice other than these two women.
screens.why5: My segment, superintendents at US general contractors, is kept word for word, and the text-message link fits how I reach supers.
screens.instead: Who should ask your superintendents the questions? Daphne is already picked; tap Saskia to hear her and switch. Recording the chosen voice once for this project uses 400 credits. Options: Daphne (picked) / Saskia.

screens.why1: Choosing how superintendents answer makes sense just before sending, but having just been asked who should ask the questions, I see Daphne offered again and it partly feels like the same choice.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but I had to reread "Every answer in a quiet room. More than 9 in 10 where it is loud" because it never says this is about the AI catching what people say.
screens.why3: I know my supers are on loud sites or in the trailer with a phone in hand, so I can judge whether they'd talk or tap.
screens.why4: Daphne, text or their choice covers it and the three are distinct, but the stray "recording" after "Hear it" and at the end of "Let them choose" reads like a broken label.
screens.why5: My pick of "Text only" is offered as is, nothing about Fresco is misstated, and naming a building site as a loud place fits my world.
screens.instead: How should superintendents answer? — Daphne, the AI interviewer: she asks aloud on video and they talk, type or tap (she catches every word in a quiet room and more than 9 in 10 on a loud site) / Text only: they read each question and tap or type / Let them choose when they open the link.

screens.why1: Once I've chosen how they answer, the obvious last step is saying who gets the link, though the 'SENT' kicker is slightly ahead of itself because nothing has gone out yet.
screens.why2: 'Who gets a link?' and 'people I know by name' are plain, but 'a search on the Contacts page' points to a page I haven't seen in this flow, so that option needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know how I reach people: superintendents and contractors I already have by name or through introductions, plus any groups where they gather.
screens.why4: The three routes (people I know, a list found with Keel, an open link for a group) are distinct and cover how I'd reach supers, and my answer is there as the first option.
screens.why5: Nothing is wrong, but the screen has lost my words: it doesn't say 'superintendents' or 'contractor operations leads', so I can't tell which group this link is for when my study needs both.
screens.instead: Who gets a link for the superintendents' interview? Options: Superintendents I know by name (I send each one their own link) / Superintendents I found with Keel (Keel makes a link for each one, and I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where superintendents already are; each person signs in with Google).

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" is plain at the top, but the number beside it is "2 of 6 holding" when the verdict is the worst dimension, so the deciding 1 of 8 at $800 sits down in the Price card and is never tied to the verdict, and the tally under it doesn't match the cards.
screens.why_b2: There is no drawn chart, and each card's line says plainly what is counted and over how many (5 of 7, 1 of 8, 3 of 8), but no bar is shown beside the numbers, so I have to work out why 3 of 8 on the pilot fails.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry the exact lines I checked, and the hours, the dollars and the $800 to $1,000 are my own numbers.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: I can't tell whether to cut the price, sell against the $1,650 to $3,300 in hours they already lose, or change the pilot, and "lower than you think" only repeats the verdict.
screens.why_b5: The tally says "1 not holding up · 3 people disagree" while the cards show one Not holding up, one People disagree and two Did not hold, so it misreports the result and reads like a count of people; 8 answers is never called a small group, "they value it below your price" reads as a general fact, and Purchase friction's "Did not hold" looks like a failure when a quick trial is good news for me.
screens.instead: Not holding up, from 8 operations leads, a small group: only 1 of 8 values it at $800 or more a site and 3 of 8 would start a paid pilot, even though most say it costs them 30+ hours a month and a trial wouldn't slow most of them, so test a lower price or tie the pilot to those hours before building on $1k.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "5 of 7 spend 30 hours or more per site a month", and that count and the median of 40 match the names listed, so I have both the answer and the deciding number.
screens.why_b2: Hours per site a month and my 30 to 60 band are plain, but I need a second look to work out why eight names became seven, and "1 said nothing" could mean Omar's blank or Faith's zero when it is Faith's zero that counts and Omar who is dropped.
screens.why_b3: The 30 to 60 hours and $1,650 to $3,300 are my numbers, but it says "the payer" rather than the contractor, and "the last thing they paid for to deal with it" doesn't fit a question about hours my trade would call the super's time.
screens.why_b4: The card never says what five of seven at 30 hours or more means for the idea, such as whether the $1k a site can lean on this cost when the price itself is failing, so I'm left to work out the next step alone.
screens.why_b5: The seven stays visible and nothing claims beyond those who answered, but the card doesn't flag how few seven is, doesn't say Omar was dropped from the count, and shows Trevor's "10.9 hours" with a precision that looks converted rather than recalled.
screens.instead: Holding up, on only 7 answers: 5 of 7 contractors put the daily log at 30 hours or more per site a month (median 40, about $2,200), one counts zero because supers do it on their own time, and one couldn't recall and isn't counted; so the cost clears the $1k price for most of them, and the next thing to find out is why they still won't pay it.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits directly above "1 of 8 at $800 or more per site a month", so I can see at once that my price failed and which number decides it.
screens.why_b2: The price bands and counts read quickly and the legend separates my band from below it, but I have to add the bars or find the 8 in the verdict line, no line says how many had to clear the price, and my $800 to $1,000 is drawn inside an $800 to $2,500 band.
screens.why_b3: Price and $800 to $1,000 per site a month are mine, but "the payer" is a generic word for the contractor, and the trailing "the last thing they paid for to deal with it" doesn't read as anything I said.
screens.why_b4: The screen stops at the verdict and never says what this means for my $1k per site, so I have to work out the options myself from the quotes, such as a free first job, pricing by active super, or showing the hours first.
screens.why_b5: It stays with the eight who answered, shows every name and how each was read, and makes no claim about contractors at large; it doesn't call eight a small group, but the 1 of 8 keeps that visible.
screens.instead: Not holding up: 1 of 8 contractor ops leads would pay $800 or more per site a month, and 5 of 8 put it under $500; eight people is a small group, but before holding $1k, test a lower or per-active-super price and bring proof of hours saved, because that is what their answers ask for.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" is stated plainly, with the deciding split right beside it: 4 of 7 from money already there, 3 needing a new line or having none.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count seven contractors by where the money came from, and Omar is shown as not counted, but I have to work out which bars count for me and no line or number shows what split would have held.
screens.why_b3: Ability to pay is recognisable as part of the money question, but the line is Keel describing its method rather than a belief of mine, and my $800 to $1k per site never appears.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what a 4-to-3 split means for selling at this price, such as whether to pitch against existing budgets or which buyers to approach first.
screens.why_b5: The counts and n stay visible and nothing is called strong, but the card says it reads my price when the answers only describe the last tool paid for, and it never says 7 is a small group.
screens.instead: People disagree: for the last tool they bought, 4 of 7 paid from money already there and 3 needed a new line or had none; this doesn't test $800 to $1k per site, so on the next calls ask which budget would cover it and expect some deals to need new sign-off.

screens.why_b1: The verdict and a number are both there, Holding up with 6 of 8, but I can't tie the 6 to the chart, where only 4 say the CFO has to agree, so I have to guess it adds the 2 who sign off alone.
screens.why_b2: The answers counted and the 8 people are easy to add up from the bars, but no bar is marked as the line, and nothing shows which bars make the 6 or what count it takes to hold.
screens.why_b3: The card's name and the line about the operations lead deciding and the CFO agreeing are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what this means for the idea, such as who to take the $800 pitch to or whether to plan for the CFO in every deal.
screens.why_b5: It says 6 of 8 went as I said when I said the CFO has to agree and only 4 said that, while 2 sign off alone and 2 name someone else, so a half-and-half result is presented as a clear hold.
screens.instead: Mixed: 4 of 8 say the CFO has to agree, 2 can sign off on $800 a site themselves and 2 say it goes to someone else or several people, so ask who signs on the first call and don't assume the CFO route.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits directly above "3 of 8 said it would take a long time", so I get the answer and the deciding number together, though not the cut-off that made 3 too few.
screens.why_b2: The three bars and the total of 8 are plain, but "You said A trial on one live job" isn't a bar, so I can't see where the line sits, and "the last thing they paid for" muddles what was asked.
screens.why_b3: "Purchase friction" and "A trial on one live job can slow or stop the purchase" are the name and belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The card doesn't say what this means for the idea, such as whether to offer a one-site trial or how to run it, so I'd have to work that out from the bars and quotes myself.
screens.why_b5: The count and n stay visible, but a flat "Did not hold" undersells a belief that only said a trial can slow a purchase when 6 of 8 would need one and 3 of 8 say it would take long, n=8 isn't called small, and "Yes, and it took a long time" reports a hypothetical as if it happened.
screens.instead: Mostly not a long delay, on a small sample: 6 of 8 would want a trial on one live job, but only 3 of 8 say it would take a long time, so plan a one-site trial and make it quick to get through, and don't treat it as a blocker.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits directly above "3 yes, 5 do not" and "3 of 8 said yes", so I get the answer and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The counts over eight people read at once, but the bar line only repeats "start a paid pilot on one site", so I have to recall for myself that I could afford no more than 1 in 3 saying probably not or no.
screens.why_b3: The title Commitment and the line about the operations lead starting a paid pilot on one site are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The card names no next step and doesn't say whether a one-site paid pilot is the wrong ask, the $1k price is the blocker, or I should go after the three who said yes.
screens.why_b5: The counts are honest and n stays visible, but eight is a small group and the card never says so, and the tail "the last thing they paid for to deal with it" muddles a question that is actually about a future pilot.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 5 of 8 operations leads would not start a paid pilot on one site, and your bar allowed at most 1 in 3; that's only eight people, but before pitching a pilot more widely, follow up with Renee, Gordon and Lena, the three who said yes, and find out what stops the other five.

screens.why_b1: Every line states its verdict, but only Buyer and payer has its deciding number (6 of 8); Price and Purchase friction show only group counts, and Commitment, the line that matters most to me, gets no verdict or number.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names are the ones I checked, but my belief lines are missing, and 'What did slow it down?' with 'Hard to justify the cost per site' drifts from my belief about a trial on one live job.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what these results mean for the idea, such as testing per-super pricing or proving the hours saved first, and it dismisses Commitment with 'nobody's follow-up landed here'.
screens.why_b5: The quotes stay with named people and nothing is claimed beyond them, but no line says n is only 8, and 'What did slow it down?' implies a real purchase and sits over answers of 'quick' or 'wouldn't be needed', with the same price quotes reused as if they were about friction.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I did not type: buyers want the hours proven first, would go higher if priced per active super, see a per-site fee stacked on their project software, ask for a free month, and worry about liability if the log is wrong in a dispute.
screens.instead: Price failed, 1 of 8 at $800 or more: buyers don't see the hours saved and dislike a per-site fee, so prove the hours on one job and test pricing per active super; the trial itself barely slowed anyone (3 of 8), and most objections to it were about cost, while 5 of 8 won't start a paid pilot now and gave no reason here.

screens.why1: As the first question it makes sense to check straight away whether my jobs run on the platforms this study cares about before asking anything else.
screens.why2: Procore and ACC are everyday words to me and the question is short, but "the construction superintendents you decide for" is a stiff way to put it, because I'd say my supers or the supers on our jobs.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our job-site software, so I know exactly which platforms our jobs run on.
screens.why4: Yes and No are distinct and a gate carries no escape, but a contractor with some jobs on Procore or ACC and some on neither has no clean answer, since "some of them" is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's Procore or ACC and nothing of a product leaks, but "you decide for" is study-writer wording that hints at how they have sorted me and my supers.
screens.why6: It is one short question that says well and ACC is spoken as letters my trade knows, but "the construction superintendents you decide for" is a mouthful on one hearing and the Yes or No options are not spoken as the template has them.
screens.instead: Do any of your company's jobs run on Procore or ACC? Yes; No

screens.why1: After confirming my jobs run on Procore or ACC, and under a heading about the buying decision, it makes sense to show me the idea I'm being asked to weigh.
screens.why2: Site walk, assignees, action items, Procore and ACC are all everyday words to me, but "AI scribe" isn't how anyone in my trade talks and "the founder's description makes no other claim" makes me stop and reread.
screens.why3: I know how my supers walk their sites, how notes and photos reach Procore or ACC, and how action items get to the crew, so I can picture this on my jobs.
screens.why4: It's a card to read, with no options, chips or box to judge.
screens.why5: The idea itself comes through clearly, but "the founder's description makes no other claim" is the study's internal paperwork showing through and tells me nothing about the product.
screens.why6: The short product sentences say well, but the closing line runs two clauses across a semicolon and ends in a stiff disclaimer that sounds odd aloud and I'd lose it on one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Fresco. During the site walk, your superintendents take short videos and talk over them. An AI turns them into notes with photos, assignees and due dates. It texts the crew their action items and sends the notes to Procore or ACC in one click. The people building it believe it would be used on the site walk.

screens.why1: Right after the idea and the question about Procore or ACC jobs, it makes sense to ask what the daily log costs us in time today before talking about buying.
screens.why2: Daily log and hours per site are the words I use every day, so I understand it on first read, though I'd have to do some math to answer.
screens.why3: My supers write the logs and nobody tracks those hours, so as the ops lead I'd be working out a rough number from about 30 to 45 minutes a day times the workdays.
screens.why4: An hours box fits and "I can't recall" is the honest way out, but "None" is odd because every site has to keep a daily log and it just duplicates typing 0.
screens.why5: It stays on the daily log, which is the real job, and no product or founder language reaches me.
screens.why6: It's one short question with one escape that I can hear once and answer, and leaving out the "None" chip costs nothing.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many hours per site did your supers spend on the daily log? Box: hours per site last month. Or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the hours my team spends on daily logs, asking what it is worth to me per site is the obvious next question for the person who pays.
screens.why2: "Worth to you a month, per site" is how I already think about job-site software costs, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our site software and know what we spend per job, so I can put a figure on this from my own budget.
screens.why4: The bands touch at $800 and $2,500 so those amounts fit two options, and "Under $500" lumps together everything from a small monthly fee to nearly $500, though the top end, the refusal and the escape are all there.
screens.why5: Fresco is named only as the idea I was shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: The question is short, but six dollar ranges read in one go, each repeating "per site a month", are too much to hold, and the guidelines say this ladder should be asked in two steps when spoken.
screens.instead: What would Fresco be worth to you a month, per site: under $800, $800 or more, or you wouldn't pay for this? Or say I can't say. If under $800: under $500, or $500 to $799? If $800 or more: $800 to $2,499, $2,500 to $5,000, or over $5,000?

screens.why1: Right after I put a number on it, asking what would make it worth more is an obvious follow-up and I can see why it comes here.
screens.why2: Plain words about a price I just gave, so I get it on first read with nothing to puzzle over.
screens.why3: I pay for these tools per job site, so I can say what would have to be true for me to pay more, such as saved super hours or fewer log disputes.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in, with no options or chips to judge.
screens.why5: Fresco was already named on the idea card I was shown on purpose, so nothing new about the product or the founder's plans reaches me here.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it is two short sentences with one question, and "$500 to $800" says easily as five hundred to eight hundred dollars.

screens.why1: Right after I put a dollar figure on it, asking how the last tool we paid for got funded is an obvious next step in a buying conversation.
screens.why2: Budget line and signed off are how I talk about money every day, so I get it on the first read or hearing.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our job site software, so I know where the money for the last tool came from.
screens.why4: The options cover the ground in my words, but 'A new budget line someone signed off' can overlap 'Taken from other spending' when a new line is funded by cutting elsewhere, and 'There was no budget for it' leaves me unsure where the money did come from.
screens.why5: It asks about my last real purchase and nothing of the founder's product or terms leaks into it.
screens.why6: Two short sentences and four short options are easy to hold after one hearing, and the escape comes last and says cleanly, though 'I can't recall one' is slightly off after 'where did the money come from'.
screens.instead: Think of the last tool your team paid for. Where did the money come from? A budget line we already had; A new budget line someone signed off; Moved over from other spending; or Paid without any budget. Or say I can't recall one.

screens.why1: I just put a price on it and said where the money comes from, so asking whether I could approve that amount myself is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Sign off, per site a month and CFO are all words I use every day, and I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our site software, so I know what I can approve and when the CFO has to agree.
screens.why4: The four answers cover the real cases, but 'I can't recall one' doesn't fit because this asks about my approval limit rather than a past event, and 'recall one' what?
screens.why5: It asks plainly who would approve the spend, uses the top of the range I gave, and doesn't bring in any product language or role labels.
screens.why6: The stem and four options are short enough to hold, but the either-or stem doesn't match the yes-and-no answers, with the Yes buried second, and 'Or say I can't recall one' sounds wrong aloud.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $800 per site a month yourself, or not? Yes, I could sign off myself; No, the CFO would have to agree; No, several people would have to agree; No, it would be someone else's decision; or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After price and who signs off, asking whether we'd want it proven on a live job before buying is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: A trial on one live job is how we talk about this, though "went through" is a little loose it's clear enough to mean the purchase got approved.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for this software, so I know whether we'd pilot it on one job first and how long that would drag on.
screens.why4: The three options cover it and the escape fits, but "a long time" and "quick" are vague, and a trial can be needed for reasons other than getting the purchase through, so "No, it wouldn't be needed" blurs a bit.
screens.why5: Fresco was named on the idea card I already read, so the name isn't a leak, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms shows through.
screens.why6: Short single question and three short options I can hold after one hearing, with the escape said last.

screens.why1: Right after asking about sign-off and a trial on a live job, asking what else would hold up the purchase is an obvious next question, though it edges close to what those two screens just covered.
screens.why2: Short and plain; I know exactly what slowing down a software purchase means at a GC, and I can answer in my own words on first hearing.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for this software, so I know what holds up a buy: IT and security review, Procore or ACC integration, contract terms, and getting supers to use it.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in, with no options or chips to judge.
screens.why5: It uses the Fresco name I was already shown on the idea card and nothing new about the product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with no symbols or parentheses, and I can hear it once and answer straight off.

screens.why1: After price, sign-off and what would slow it down, asking whether I'd actually start a paid pilot is the obvious closing question.
screens.why2: A paid pilot on one site is how I'd talk about trying any jobsite software, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: Whether to pay for a pilot on one of my sites is exactly the call I make in this job.
screens.why4: The three options cover it, but the ladder is lopsided: a full-sentence yes against a bare 'Probably not' and 'No', with no 'Probably yes' or 'Yes, if the price is right' for where I'd really land, and 'Probably not' and 'No' sit close together.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose, and a paid pilot on one site reads as a plain commitment question with nothing else of the founder's plan or terms for people reaching me.
screens.why6: Short, one question and three options I can hold, though saying the yes option repeats most of the question I just heard.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you start a paid pilot on one site, or not? Yes, I'd start one; Probably, depending on the price; Probably not; or No.
